subject: Chemistry
title: Coordination Compounds
summary: A coordination compound has a central metal atom/ion bonded to ligands (Lewis bases) through coordinate bonds, e.g. [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃. The number of donor atoms bonded is the coordination number.
Werner's theory: metals have primary valence (oxidation state, ionisable) and secondary valence (coordination number, directional, non-ionisable).

Valence bond theory explains geometry and magnetism by hybridisation; crystal field theory explains colour and magnetism by splitting of d orbitals (Δₒ) — strong-field ligands cause pairing (low spin).
Isomerism (structural: ionisation, linkage, coordination, hydrate; stereo: geometrical, optical) and IUPAC naming are the most-asked parts.

formulas.name: Oxidation state of the metal
formulas.formula: charge of complex = metal oxidation state + Σ ligand charges
formulas.note: Neutral ligands (NH₃, H₂O, CO, en) contribute 0.

formulas.name: Coordination number
formulas.formula: CN = number of donor atoms attached (bidentate en counts 2, EDTA⁴⁻ counts 6)

formulas.name: Spectrochemical series
formulas.formula: I⁻ < Br⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < S²⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < C₂O₄²⁻ < H₂O < NCS⁻ < EDTA⁴⁻ < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO
formulas.note: CN⁻ and CO are strong-field (cause pairing); halides are weak-field.

formulas.name: CFT splitting (octahedral)
formulas.formula: t₂g (3 orbitals, −0.4Δₒ each) and e_g (2 orbitals, +0.6Δₒ each)

formulas.name: CFSE
formulas.formula: CFSE = (−0.4 x + 0.6 y) Δₒ (+ pairing energies);  x = t₂g, y = e_g electrons

formulas.name: High spin vs low spin
formulas.formula: Δₒ < P → high spin (weak field);  Δₒ > P → low spin (strong field)

formulas.name: Tetrahedral splitting
formulas.formula: Δₜ = (4/9) Δₒ;  almost always high spin

formulas.name: VBT hybridisation and geometry
formulas.formula: sp³ tetrahedral;  dsp² square planar;  sp³d² octahedral (outer orbital, high spin);  d²sp³ octahedral (inner orbital, low spin)

formulas.name: Geometrical isomers
formulas.formula: MA₄B₂ (octahedral): 2 (cis, trans);  MA₃B₃: 2 (fac, mer);  MA₂B₂ square planar: 2;  tetrahedral: none

formulas.name: Optical isomers
formulas.formula: [M(AA)₃] (e.g. [Co(en)₃]³⁺): 2 enantiomers;  cis-[M(AA)₂B₂] is optically active, trans is not

formulas.name: Werner's theory
formulas.formula: primary valence = oxidation state (satisfied by anions, ionisable);  secondary valence = CN (fixed geometry)
formulas.when: Interpreting AgCl precipitation and conductance data.

examples.title: Low-spin iron(III)
examples.solution: Fe³⁺ d⁵, CN⁻ strong field → t₂g⁵ (1 unpaired) → μ = √3 ≈ 1.73 BM (d²sp³).

examples.title: High-spin iron(III)
examples.solution: F⁻ weak field → t₂g³e_g² (5 unpaired) → μ = √35 ≈ 5.92 BM (sp³d²).

examples.title: CFSE of [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺
examples.problem: Co³⁺ is d⁶; NH₃ makes it low spin. CFSE (ignore pairing energy)?

examples.title: Counting stereoisomers
examples.solution: trans (optically inactive) + cis (a pair of enantiomers) = 3.

examples.title: Werner's data
examples.problem: 1 mol of CoCl₃·6NH₃ gives 3 mol AgCl with excess AgNO₃. Formula?

examples.title: IUPAC name
examples.solution: Potassium trioxalatoferrate(III): ligands alphabetically with prefixes, anionic complex ends in -ate (ferrate), oxidation state in Roman numerals.

topics.title: Key terms
topics.explain: Ligand: ion or molecule donating an electron pair (monodentate NH₃, Cl⁻; bidentate en, C₂O₄²⁻; polydentate EDTA⁴⁻). Ambidentate ligands bind through two different atoms (NO₂⁻/ONO⁻, SCN⁻/NCS⁻). Chelate: ring formed by a polydentate ligand — extra stable (chelate effect).

topics.title: IUPAC naming rules
topics.explain: Cation before anion. Inside the bracket: ligands in alphabetical order (ignoring di/tri prefixes), then metal with oxidation state in Roman numerals. Anionic ligands end in -o (chlorido, cyanido, oxalato); neutral: aqua, ammine, carbonyl. Anionic complexes use -ate names (ferrate, cuprate, argentate, aurate, plumbate).

topics.title: Structural isomerism
topics.explain: Ionisation: [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ vs [Co(NH₃)₅SO₄]Br. Linkage: M–NO₂ vs M–ONO. Coordination: exchange of ligands between cationic and anionic complexes. Hydrate (solvate): [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ (violet) vs [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O (green).

topics.title: Colour of complexes
topics.explain: Light of a certain energy (= Δ) excites an electron from t₂g to e_g; we see the complementary colour. [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is violet. Without ligands (anhydrous CuSO₄) there is no splitting, so it is white.

topics.title: Limitations of VBT and CFT
topics.explain: VBT doesn't explain colour or the strength of ligands. CFT treats ligands as point charges and cannot explain why neutral CO is a strong ligand — that needs metal–ligand π back-bonding (as in metal carbonyls like Ni(CO)₄, Fe(CO)₅).

topics.title: Importance and applications
topics.explain: Haemoglobin (Fe), chlorophyll (Mg), vitamin B₁₂ (Co) are coordination compounds. EDTA is used to measure water hardness and treat lead poisoning; cis-platin is an anticancer drug; complexes are used in metallurgy (gold extraction with CN⁻) and analysis (Ni²⁺ with dimethylglyoxime).

topics.title: Very stable complexes hide the metal ion
topics.explain: If a complex is very stable, so little free metal ion is left that its usual tests fail. Cu²⁺ with excess CN⁻ gives a cyano complex — actually Cu(I): 2Cu²⁺ + 10CN⁻ → 2[Cu(CN)₄]³⁻ + (CN)₂ (NCERT writes it as K₂[Cu(CN)₄]). Either way H₂S then gives NO CuS precipitate. Also, Cu does not liberate H₂ from dilute HCl (E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V).

ratta: Oxidation state from charge balance; CN = donor atoms.
Strong field: CN⁻, CO, en, NH₃;  weak: I⁻, Br⁻, Cl⁻, F⁻.
d²sp³ inner, low spin;  sp³d² outer, high spin;  dsp² square planar.
CuSO₄ + excess KCN → stable cyano complex [Cu(CN)₄]³⁻ → no CuS with H₂S.
